title: Cargo Bay Calibration
subtitle: Length, Volume, Weight & Mass
tagline: The inventory robot's sensors are glitching. Recalibrate the scanner before the cargo bay overflows.

slides.headline: Warning: Sensor Malfunction
body: A heavy cargo ship just docked, but our inventory robot is completely glitching out. It's trying to measure the volume of a wrench and the length of our coolant water!
The Math Cadet needs to take manual control of the Cargo Scanner and recalibrate every sensor — length, volume, weight, and mass — before the whole bay goes offline.

image.alt: An inventory robot stands beside cargo crates, its sensor display glitching with error symbols while an amber warning light flashes above.

slides.headline: Four properties. Four scanners.
slides.intro: Before you calibrate, you need to know which property to check — and which unit system goes with it. Use the **Measurement Graphic Organizer** as your reference.

cards.name: Length
cards.description: How long, wide, or far something is.

cards.name: Volume
cards.description: How much space a liquid fills.

cards.name: Weight
cards.description: How heavy something feels on Earth. **Customary system.**

cards.name: Mass
cards.description: How much matter is inside an object. **Metric system.**

image.alt: Four holographic sensor panels in a row showing icons for length (ruler), volume (beaker), weight (balance scale), and mass (digital scale).

prompt.question: Calibrate the scanner for this item.

correct.title: Lock Confirmed!
body: We use **Meters** (metric) or **Feet** (customary) to measure length. Reference: 1 Foot = 12 Inches, 1 Meter = 100 cm.

config.instruction: Select what property to measure, then lock in the correct unit scale.
config.hint: A cargo door is pretty tall. You wouldn't want to measure it in tiny millimeters, but a kilometer is way too big.

correct.title: Weight Confirmed!
body: Weight is a **customary** measurement. Ounces for small items (a slice of bread ≈ 1 oz), **Pounds** for mid-weight items, Tons for vehicles or shipping containers. Reference: 1 Pound = 16 Ounces, 1 Ton = 2,000 Pounds.

config.instruction: Lock in the correct property and unit for weighing this crate.
config.hint: A supply crate is heavy, but not vehicle-heavy. 1 Ton = 2,000 pounds — way more than one crate.

correct.title: Mass Logged!
body: Mass is a **metric** measurement — **Kilograms** for heavy objects, Grams for a paperclip, Milligrams for medicine doses. 1 kg = 1,000 g. (Remember: Weight uses pounds — Mass uses kilograms.)

config.instruction: Lock in the correct property and unit for measuring something heavy.
config.hint: An engine is very heavy. You need the biggest unit of mass on this list.

correct.title: Volume Locked!
body: **Liters** (metric) and **Gallons** (customary) both measure volume. 1 Liter = 10 Deciliters; 1 Gallon = 4 Quarts. Milliliters are way too small for a tank — you'd use those for a spoonful of medicine.

config.instruction: Lock in the correct property and unit for measuring a large liquid tank.
config.hint: A tank holds a lot of liquid. Think about a large soda bottle — bigger than a milliliter, smaller than a gallon-sized jug.

slides.headline: The Reasonableness Check
slides.intro: Even when the robot picks the right unit, the number might be totally wrong. Always ask yourself: **Does this make sense?**

rows.name: The "Too Big" Trap
rows.description: Logging a coffee cup as holding 5 Liters. (A 2-Liter soda bottle is huge — a coffee cup is much smaller!).

counter.label: CHECK
counter.text: Is the number too big for real life?

rows.name: The "Too Small" Trap
rows.description: Logging a spacesuit's **mass** as 5 grams. (A nickel has a mass of about 5 grams!).

counter.label: CHECK
counter.text: Is the number too small for real life?

image.alt: Two side-by-side scanner displays — one showing a coffee cup with an absurdly huge volume readout, the other showing a spacesuit with an absurdly tiny mass readout — both flagged with warning symbols.

prompt.scenario:
**📋 CARGO MANIFEST — PENDING REVIEW**

The inventory robot just submitted this manifest. One of these log entries is definitely BROKEN. Perform a Reasonableness Check and flag the error.
prompt.question: Which log entry is broken?

correct.title: Log Deleted!
body: Exactly! A single water bottle does not hold 400 liters (that's like a small swimming pool). The robot messed up.

opt-a.title: That one is fine!
body: A wrench is about 15 centimeters long (a bit shorter than a standard ruler). Try checking the other logs.

opt-b.title: That one is fine!
body: An adult astronaut with a mass of 80 kilograms makes perfect sense. Check the other logs.

opt-d.title: Close — but not the broken one.
body: A shipping container at 2 ounces IS wrong (they weigh tons!), but there's an even MORE obviously broken log. Keep looking.

wrongDefault.title: Math Trap
body: Think about how big these objects are in real life.

slides.headline: Mission Complete
slides.subtext: Length, volume, weight, and mass — every scanner is green. The cargo bay is fully supplied. Keep the Measurement Graphic Organizer handy for your next calibration run.

image.alt: A fully stocked cargo bay with neat rows of labeled crates, calm cyan lighting, and the inventory robot standing confidently with a steady checkmark on its display.
